analysis.one_liner: Cuts the top corporate income tax rate from 35% to 25%.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee when the 2008 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have lowered the top federal corporate income tax rate by 10 percentage points, from 35% to 25%, including for personal service corporations like law and consulting firms. The bill offered no way to replace the roughly $100 billion-plus per year in revenue the federal government would have given up. It was referred to the tax-writing committee and never received any hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Large profitable corporations and their shareholders would have seen their federal income tax bills drop substantially. Corporations taxed at the top 35% rate would have kept an additional 10 cents of every dollar of taxable profit; owners of pass-through-adjacent service firms organized as personal service corporations would have gained the same cut.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Internal Revenue Code to reduce the maximum corporate income tax rate from 35% to 25%, and applies the same reduction to personal service corporations [S2][S3].

The bill was introduced as a stimulus-style measure during the January 2008 economic downturn, framing the corporate rate cut as a way to encourage investment and job growth in the United States [S1].
The cut would apply to taxable years beginning after enactment, with conforming changes to the 30% withholding rate on certain foreign payments reduced to 25% [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers in general would bear the cost: the roughly 10-point rate cut would have reduced federal revenue by well over $100 billion per year, with no offsetting tax increases or spending cuts in the bill. Unless matched by other changes, that gap would have been filled by borrowing, by future cuts to government services, or by higher taxes elsewhere.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no revenue offset; the entire cost of cutting the corporate rate from 35% to 25% would have been added to the deficit or displaced other public spending, with the direct benefit flowing to corporate shareholders rather than to wage earners [S2][S3].

The benefit would concentrate among the most profitable corporations and their owners; companies already paying low effective rates (through credits and deductions) would gain far less than top-bracket payers, and workers would only benefit to the extent that firms reinvested the savings in jobs rather than shareholder payouts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main promise — that cutting the corporate rate would spur investment and jobs — rested on the assumption that corporations would pass their tax savings to workers and expansion rather than to shareholders. The direct, certain effect was a large transfer of federal revenue to profitable corporations, with nothing in the bill requiring job creation or covering the cost. An honest weighing finds the cost concrete and immediate, the promised benefit indirect and uncertain.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the two-year Congress ended in January 2009, never receiving a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Eric Cantor (R-VA) introduced the bill on January 29, 2008, during the onset of the recession, as a proposal to cut the top corporate tax rate from 35% to 25% [S1][S2].
The bill attracted just one cosponsor, a fellow House Republican [S4].

It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction; that is the only action recorded for the bill, which received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers kept the roughly 10-point corporate rate's worth of revenue, since the cut was never enacted; large profitable corporations and their shareholders are worse off in the narrow sense that the 10-point tax cut never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers; corporations missed the cut

for.name: Rep. Eric Cantor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 29, 2008, proposing to cut the top corporate rate from 35% to 25%

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, and no vote on the bill before the Congress ended

against.name: Rep. Charles Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was entirely Republican — Rep. Cantor plus one Republican cosponsor — and with Democrats holding the House majority and the Ways and Means chairmanship, the bill got no committee action.

industries.industry: Large profitable corporations and their shareholders
industries.note: The bill would have cut the top corporate tax rate by 10 percentage points, a direct transfer of federal revenue to top-bracket corporations and their owners, with no offset or requirement of job creation. The cost would have fallen on the general taxpayer through the deficit or reduced public spending.

industries.industry: Personal service corporations (law, accounting, consulting firms)
industries.note: The bill explicitly cuts the top rate for personal service corporations from 35% to 25%, extending the benefit to high-earning professional firms organized as corporations.
